title: Psalm 81: If Only My People Would Listen
summary: A festival call to worship summons Israel to sing, play instruments, and sound the ram's horn at the New Moon and the full moon, as God commanded. Then God himself speaks, recalling how he freed his people from slavery in Egypt and tested them at Meribah, repeating the first commandment, and lamenting that they would not listen. He promises that if they would walk in his ways, he would subdue their enemies and feed them with the finest wheat and honey from the rock.
story: Psalm 81 follows the pleas for restoration in Psalms 79 and 80 with a word from God that addresses the root of Israel's troubles: they did not listen. It stands with Psalms 50 and 95 as a festival psalm in which a call to worship gives way to a divine sermon, and it reads like a condensed version of Deuteronomy, recalling the exodus, the wilderness testing, and the command to have no other gods. Its question for the reader is whether worship will be joined with obedience. Psalm 82, which follows, extends the theme of divine judgment from Israel to the gods and rulers of the nations.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. Of Asaph.” Gittith also appears in the headings of Psalms 8 and 84. Its meaning is uncertain; suggestions include an instrument or tune associated with the Philistine city of Gath, or a song connected with the wine press (the Hebrew gat), which would fit an autumn harvest festival. For Asaph and his guild of Levitical singers, see Psalm 73.

The festival in verse 3 is debated. The New Moon marked the start of each month, and the full moon fell in the middle of it. Many scholars connect the psalm with the seventh month, when the Feast of Trumpets was held at the new moon (Leviticus 23:24; Numbers 29:1) and the Feast of Tabernacles began at the full moon on the fifteenth day (Leviticus 23:34). Others connect it with Passover, which also began at the full moon, on the fifteenth of the first month, and which fits the psalm's focus on the exodus. The Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish tradition compiled around AD 200, lists Psalm 81 as the psalm the Levites sang in the temple on the fifth day of the week. The psalm's date of composition is unknown; its references to Joseph in verse 5 have led some scholars to link its origins to the northern kingdom, while others see Joseph as a name for all Israel in Egypt.
cultural:
Israel's festivals were loud and joyful. The instruments of verse 2 include the tambourine (a hand drum often played by women, as by Miriam in Exodus 15:20), the harp, and the lyre. The ram's horn, or shofar, was blown to announce festivals, gather the people, and sound alarms. It was not a musical instrument in the modern sense but a signal. The festivals were statutes and ordinances (verse 4), commanded by God and rooted in Israel's history.

The burden and the basket of verse 6 recall the forced labor in Egypt, where Israelites carried bricks and clay (Exodus 1:11-14). The cloud of thunder (verse 7) recalls God's appearing at Sinai. Meribah, meaning quarreling, was the place where the people tested God by demanding water (Exodus 17:1-7; Numbers 20:1-13). Honey from the rock (verse 16) echoes the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:13) and pictures abundance even in rocky, barren places, perhaps wild bees nesting in rock crevices.
literary: The psalm has two unequal parts. Verses 1 to 5 are a call to worship addressed to the congregation. At the end of verse 5 a new voice enters (an unfamiliar language), and from verse 6 to the end God speaks in the first person, probably through a priest or prophet during the festival. God's speech recalls the exodus (verses 6 and 7), restates the first commandment (verses 8 to 10), laments Israel's refusal to listen (verses 11 and 12), and closes with a conditional promise (verses 13 to 16). The key word is listen or hear (shama), which appears in verses 8, 11, and 13. The words “if only” (verses 8 and 13) express God's longing rather than mere command. Verse 10 echoes the opening of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2).

outline.t: Call to worship at the festival
God recalls freeing Israel from slavery
No foreign god: I am the LORD your God
If only they would walk in My ways

doctrines.note: Verses 9 and 10 restate the first commandment and its basis: God brought Israel out of Egypt. His law flows from his saving act and calls for exclusive loyalty.
The psalm forbids any strange or foreign god. Israel's troubles are traced not to enemies but to divided loyalty and refusal to listen to God.
Verse 12 describes God giving his people over to their own stubborn hearts. Sometimes God's judgment is simply letting people have their way and live with the results.

words.note: Shama, to hear, listen, or obey. Hebrew doesn't sharply separate hearing from obeying: to truly hear is to respond. God's lament in verses 11 and 13 is that his people would not listen, meaning they would not obey.

Shophar, the ram's horn. It was blown to mark festivals, call assemblies, and signal battle. In verse 3 it announces the New Moon and the feast. Jews still sound the shofar at the new year and on the Day of Atonement.

Sheririt, stubbornness or hardness. In verse 12 God gives his people over to the stubbornness of their hearts. The word is used often in Jeremiah (for example 7:24) for Israel's persistent refusal to listen.

Meribah, meaning quarreling or strife. It was the place where Israel tested God by demanding water. Here God says he tested them there (verse 7), and the name became a byword for unbelief (compare Psalm 95:8).

christ: Psalm 81 isn't quoted directly in the New Testament, and its connection to Jesus is thematic. God's lament, “if only you would listen to Me”, echoes in Jesus' lament over Jerusalem, which would not come to him (Matthew 23:37). At the transfiguration the Father's voice says of Jesus, “Listen to Him” (Mark 9:7), making listening to Jesus the form that listening to God now takes. Paul's description of God giving people over to the desires of their hearts (Romans 1:24) echoes verse 12. And the promise to satisfy his people with the finest wheat is fulfilled in Jesus, who calls himself the bread of life (John 6:35).

hard.q: What does it mean that God gave his people up to their stubborn hearts?
hard.a: Verse 12 describes a form of judgment in which God stops restraining people and lets them follow their own path. Some readers find this troubling because it seems to mean God abandons people. The psalm itself frames it as a response to persistent refusal: God called, warned, and pleaded, and his people would not listen. Interpreters in different traditions stress different things. Some emphasize God's sovereignty in hardening, others human responsibility for refusing, and many hold both together, as Scripture often does. What the psalm makes clear is that the verdict is not God's desire; the very next verse repeats his longing, if only My people would listen to Me.

questions: The psalm moves from joyful festival worship to God's rebuke. How can worship go on while people are not listening to God?
God reminds Israel that he freed them from slavery before calling them to obey. How does remembering what God has done shape your obedience?
Verse 10 says, “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.” Where are you looking for satisfaction outside of God?
